title: Explosive & Hostile Events: Blast, Active Shooter, TECC
learningObjectives: Classify blast injuries (primary to quinary) and recognize blast lung.
Apply TECC phases of care and the THREAT sequence.
Explain the Rescue Task Force model and casualty collection points.
Anticipate secondary devices, upside-down triage, and responder targeting.

summary.title: Blast Injury Classes
summary.content: PRIMARY: the pressure wave hits air-filled organs — tympanic membranes, lungs (blast lung), bowel; worse in ENCLOSED spaces and near the device. SECONDARY: fragments/shrapnel/debris — the most common cause of blast injuries (penetrating wounds anywhere, eyes). TERTIARY: the body thrown, or structure collapsing on it — blunt trauma, traumatic amputation, crush. QUATERNARY: everything else — burns, toxic inhalation, CO, exacerbation of chronic illness. QUINARY: hyperinflammatory state from additives (bacteria, chemicals, radiation).

summary.title: Blast Lung & Blast Pearls
summary.content: Blast lung: dyspnea, hypoxia, cough, hemoptysis, chest pain — can appear up to 24–48 h later. Give O2, avoid aggressive fluids, be careful with positive-pressure ventilation (pneumothorax and arterial air embolism risk), watch for tension pneumothorax. A ruptured eardrum signals significant pressure exposure but is NOT a reliable marker of blast lung — and an intact eardrum doesn't rule it out. Victims may be deafened: communicate with gestures and written cues. Traumatic amputation = high energy; look for hidden torso injury.

summary.title: Hostile MCI: The Threat Changes Everything
summary.content: Active shooters, bombings, vehicle rammings, and complex coordinated attacks may target responders. Expect secondary devices near CCPs and staging, shooters moving between locations, and fake 'victims'. Staging out of sight; vary your positions; no gathering in obvious open spaces; police cordons decide where you can go. 'Upside-down triage': the least injured flee and self-present to nearby hospitals first; the critically injured arrive later via EMS.

summary.title: TECC — Three Phases of Care
summary.content: DIRECT THREAT (hot): win the fight / get out of the line of fire; casualty self-aid if possible; ONLY tourniquet for life-threatening extremity bleeding ('high and tight') and move to cover — no airway management, no spinal immobilization. INDIRECT THREAT (warm): structured MARCH care — reassess/convert tourniquets, pack junctional wounds, recovery position/NPA, chest seal and needle decompression, prevent hypothermia, consider TXA per protocol, prepare for movement. EVACUATION (cold): reassess and continue care during transport; more advanced interventions as resources allow.

summary.title: THREAT & the Rescue Task Force
summary.content: Hartford Consensus THREAT: Threat suppression, Hemorrhage control, Rapid Extrication to safety, Assessment by medical providers, Transport to definitive care. Rescue Task Force (RTF): small teams of EMS/fire in ballistic protection, escorted by law enforcement, entering CLEARED warm-zone areas to stop bleeding and move casualties to a casualty collection point (CCP) — while other officers keep hunting the threat. Goal: 'Stop the killing, then stop the dying.' Bystanders with Stop the Bleed training save lives before you arrive.

clinicalPearls: Hemorrhage is the leading preventable cause of death in hostile events — tourniquets early, high and tight in the hot zone.
In direct threat, the best medicine is fire superiority and cover — not airway management.
Enclosed-space blasts (bus, train, room) produce far more primary blast injury than open-air blasts.
Every ruptured eardrum is a reason to look harder at the lungs — but a normal eardrum doesn't clear them.
CCPs and staging are predictable targets — ask police to clear them for secondary devices.
redFlags: Unattended bags, vehicles parked oddly near the scene, or a second explosion.
Responders bunching at one obvious spot (perfect secondary target).
Delayed dyspnea or hypoxia in a blast survivor who looked fine (blast lung).
Aggressive fluids or high-pressure ventilation in blast lung.
commonMistakes: Entering a hot zone without law enforcement — or not entering cleared warm zones when RTF is the plan.
Using a tourniquet too low or too loose in the hot zone ('high and tight' then reassess in warm).
Assuming an intact eardrum rules out primary blast injury.
Forgetting the tourniquet time on the tag.
memoryAids: Blast classes: 1 Pressure, 2 Projectiles, 3 Pushed/Pinned, 4 Plus everything else (burns, toxins), 5 Pro-inflammatory.
THREAT: Threat suppression, Hemorrhage control, Rapid Extrication, Assessment, Transport.
TECC: Hot = Tourniquet & Cover; Warm = MARCH; Cold = Reassess & Ride.

decisionTrees.title: Hostile Event — EMS Flow
decisionTrees.content:
Report of shooting/explosion
  → Stage out of sight; police establish cordons
  → Threat ongoing? Direct threat = HOT → police only (self-aid/TQ by those already inside)
  → Areas cleared but not secure = WARM → Rescue Task Forces with police escort:
       TQs, packing, airway positioning, chest seals → move to CCP
  → CCP → triage (SALT/START) → COLD treatment & transport
  → Watch for secondary devices; re-check staging/CCP safety
